messages.subject: Variance estimation in strip census
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

I've been working on the following issue for too many days now, so looking for some outside help. I'm analyzing the results of an aerial survey using photography. I have four strata with two of them having various numbers of sightings, and two without sightings. The maximum observation width of each images from the trackline is 500 m to both sides, so in total there is 1km coverage. We assume all objects are detected so I'm considering this as a strip census, and try to analyze the data manually.

I'm getting stuck on estimating the variance of the density. Equation 3.123 in Introduction to Distance Sampling (Buckland et al. 2009) seems to be appropriate but I'm not sure what to do with the var[h(0)] terms.

Also, on page 90 it states that var(N) = A2*var(D). However, in all the output of Distance the variance of the D is identical to the variance of N, so not sure if I should indeed multiply by area square?

Any help would be appreciated!

thanks,

Koen Broker

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Variance estimation in strip census
messages.body_plain:
Koen

Estimation of precision for a strip transect is described in Buckland et al. (2015) in section 6.2.1.  Notation is "se" means standard error, n/L is average detection rate across transects and w is transect half width (500m in your case).  Uncertainty in your density estimate is variability in encounter rates between transects; there is no uncertainty in any facet of detectability because detectability is assumed known (and perfect).

Eqn 3.123 from Buckland et al. (2001) is referring to point transect sampling, hence h(0) is a parameter associated with the detection function, which does not exist when using strip transects.  In your original message, it is unclear whether what you call "strata" are actually transects.

messages.body_plain:
Sara

As Piotr notes, we suspect you wish to analyse data from a strip transect survey (perfect detectability out to some truncation distance).  We also suspect you have a number of these transects, rather than just a single transect.

You enter the data.  If the data are from a strip transect survey, then you likely have not recorded perpendicular distances.  That is fine, you can simple enter some constant value of 2.5 (if that is your truncation distance) for the perpendicular distances.  Distance wants to fit a detection function to the data, but if they are from a strip transect survey, you will want to fit a uniform key function with NO adjustment terms.  This will produce a detection function that remains at 1 out to the truncation distance.

If those instructions are no sufficient, please ask for further details.

Hi All,

two days back at work after workshop last week and have a new distance project on my desk already!

The field survey team have designed new survey with the intention of sampling on just one side of the transect line (due to issues of surface glare making detecting seabirds on surface difficult).  I've said to include both sides, mainly to reduce risk of getting a small sample size, and we can then include a proxy for surface glare as a covariate when we run Distance. I don't think that there will be issues with increased uncertainty when extrapolating to a larger area, as study is based on 2 visits, each visit comprising 25x transects, 6km long, 1km apart, within a study area of 6x25km.

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Papy

Sampling plans (what we call survey designs) can be created in the Distance software using the "survey design engine".  The design engine is the subject of Chapter 6 in the Users Guide that is provided with the Distance software.  There are two "quick start" explanations in Chapter 3 of the guide--showing how to bring a shapefile of the study area into Distance and examine various survey designs.  The second example, designing a survey for northwestern states of Mexico, forms the basis for a Distance project "Mexico" that is included with the distribution of the software.

Distance includes a rudimentary GIS system inside it called MapTools; it is not a full-blown GIS system, but provides the basics to be able to randomly place survey effort into your study area, which is the basis of being able to draw inference from your survey.

messages.body_plain:
Colin

Happy to know you're back at your desk, complete with a new sampling project.

The topic of one-sided transects is something we did not discuss last week, but there is a figure on p. 118 in the introductory notes we provided to you

I agree with you exhorting the crew to exert effort on both sides and cope with glare (or side) perhaps as a covariate.  The difficulty with one-sided transects is the influence of uncertainty regarding whether an animal is just outside the strip (meaning it is not recorded) or just inside the strip (meaning it enters the data with a very small perpendicular distance).  The propensity of observers is to record detections, hence the potential exists to (as the slide notes) create a spike at zero distance.  As you learned last week, from watching Len work with the blue monkey dataset, fitting a detection to data with a spike at zero distance is not pleasant.

messages.subject: Truncation Distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I hope everyone is fine.
I work in a small reserve in South Africa (9x7.6km2), where different ungulates are kept. The reserve is rounded by a fence that animals cannot jump through, making it a small island in the middle of the land. I would like to build a DSM for modelling spatial density of ungulates inside the reserve. I have 8 line transects that go from west to east and vice versa, and are separated by 950m from each other. Transects 1 and 8 are 475m away from north and south fences. I only walk 1 transect per day, so the 8 transects are walked in a 2 weeks period.
Due to I want to build DSM, I segmented my transects by 500m.

My question is about which truncation you recommend I should choose to estimate the detectability curve, considering that my longest detection is 1.4km away fron transect...

1. If I exclude the 5% of the distance data, my truncation distance is around 800m, but this means that the area of different transects are spatially overlapping, hence some segments are overlapping (e.g. An animal detected 800m North of T4 is 150m south of T3). Nevertheless histograms and detection curves have the "typical" shape of these models (detectability decreases with distance).

2. If I choose the truncation to be 475m, areas of different transects are not overlapping, but I have to exclude around half of the data and histograms shows that detectability decreases only a "little bit" with distance (due to I work with large mammals, with this distance the detectability at 475m keeps high).

I would like to use the first option (better plots and more data), but I dont know if that is correct. or... Should I eliminate some transects? I don't know, what do you recommend for this situation?
Thank you so much
Regards

Nicolas

Good questions.  My arithmetic suggests you have somewhere in the vicinity of ~120 segments after you break your 8 ~7.6km transects into 500m segments. This is actually a fairly small number as this constitutes the sample size with which you will be building your GAMs.   For that reason, I don't think I'd suggest eliminating transects.

As a first approximation, it is customary to have segment length equal to twice truncation distance--resulting in segments being roughly square.  That would suggest truncating your data further than your two suggestions--resulting in what would effectively be strip transects.  But that seems preferable to segments where detections are closest to adjacent transects.  Under the situation you describe in your point numbered 1, it is not clear to me that environmental covariates associated with T4 (where the detection was made) would provide better explanatory power than covariates from T3 (which is closer to the animal's locations).

Density surface models are generally used where the proportion of the study area sampled is small, rather than the situation you describe where the proportion of the area surveyed is >1 (because covered region of adjacent transects overlap).

messages.subject: Extreme heaping in detection functions
messages.body_plain:
Dear distance samplers,

I have an interesting situation that I hope to get your opinion on. Sorry for the long writeup. Thanks to anyone who goes through it. Opinions of any length are welcome; no need to write this much in return.

First some background:

I’m working on detection functions the U.S. NOAA North Atlantic Right Whale Sighting Survey (NARWSS). This is an aerial survey flown at 750 ft altitude with Twin Otter aircraft. Its primary mission is not distance sampling, but to find right whales to photograph for a photo ID census and derived population size estimates. Nonetheless the program uses sawtooth survey designs, collects vertical angles with inclinometers, and is otherwise generally compatible with the requirements for distance sampling. The observers are highly trained and also work on other surveys explicitly designed for broad-scale density analysis (e.g. the NOAA “AMAPPS” surveys) flown on the same aircraft by the same organization. This survey has provided year-round coverage of its study area for over 15 years, with surveying performed in every season of every year, making it essentially irreplaceable for what I’m doing.

All is not perfect however. The aircraft have large bubble windows but on NARWSS surveys there are only two window observers; there is no belly observer, nor a second team, precluding an mrds analysis. That is ok; we can do a single-team analysis. Of greater concern, the protocol asks observers to spend less time guarding the trackline than is proper for distance sampling, and more time looking in the distance for whales. This is intended to maximize the number of right whales they can find and go photograph, Unfortunately histograms of sighting distances suggest this practice causes them to miss some animals along the trackline. We have dealt with this problem with left truncation.

And there is another caveat, the one I would like your opinion on:

Because NARWSS has flown so many surveys (roughly 0.5 million linear km on effort) and the protocol allows observers to spend some of their time looking into the distance, they have obtained quite a few sightings at distances that might be farther than is typical for aerial surveys flown at 750 ft. Assuming these sightings can be incorporated into a detection function reasonably well, I would like to retain as many of them as possible, as I am trying to fit seasonal density surface GAMs with multiple covariates. These GAMs work best when many sightings are available.

The complication is that there is some heaping of vertical angles, which is exacerbated by the relatively large angles obtained for distant sightings. Below 80 degrees, there was a tendency to heap at 5 degree increments. This stopped at 80 degrees but the inclinometer only had a resolution of 1 degree, yielding measurements of 80, 81, 82, and so on. At those extreme angles, a 1 degree angular difference corresponds to a large linear distance range on the ground.

(Now, some of you are probably already thinking that this is crazy, trying to utilize aerial sightings with vertical angles of 80 degrees and even higher. Feel free to tell me so, but please bear with me and see what results. Then tell me again it is crazy, if desired.)

The attached heaping.png histogram of sightings of right whales by distance shows what I’m talking about. The x axis is distance in meters; the y axis is count of sightings. The "spikes" in this histogram correspond to vertical angles which I have labelled in red. At 80 degrees and higher, the clustering that occurs around the spike results from variations in aircraft altitude, not in the sighing angle. If the aircraft were flown at precisely the target altitude at all times, the clusters would shrink to perfect spikes at the heaping distances, with nothing at intermediate distances. Below 80 degrees, the clustering around the 5 degree increments results both from variation in altitude and from not all measurements being rounded to 5 degrees.

>From the height of these spikes, you can see why I would want to retain them, if possible: they represent a very large number of sightings that I’d like to make available to the spatial modeling stage, if possible. In the right whale example, there are roughly 700 sightings in the 80-87 degree range, out of 1700 total. I am reluctant to discard many of those, if they can be reasonably retained. This leads to two questions:

1. Do these represent a long tail that is hard to model well and should thus be truncated?

2. Assuming they can be modeled reasonably, should I fit detection functions with explicit breaks to account for the heaping, or not?

To address the first question, let’s assume the answer is Yes and examine resulting detection functions to see if they are reasonable. For this example, I’ll use a detection function for fin and sei whales rather than for right whales. The attached LeftTrunc.pdf shows the sightings I used. I left truncated these at 62 m, an angle of 15 degrees at 750 ft, based on examining this plot. This is an area of the trackline that was not sufficiently attended. The red bar represents the truncated sightings.

I right truncated at 3738 m, an angle of 86.5 degrees, with the intent of enclosing the bin that was centered on 86 degrees. Conceptually, this assumes the error in angular measurement was spread evenly between 85.5 and 86.5 degrees. This discarded 341 sightings, 11% of the total, that were beyond this distance, leaving 2608 left, 87% of the total. This right-truncates considerably more than 5%, which is suggested in various places as a general rule.

The attached NoBins.pdf and NoBins.txt show the resulting detection function. I used the species identification as an MCDS covariate to deal with the problem that many sightings were reported as “fin or sei whale” because observers are less likely to be able to distinguish between the two as distance increases (but are still able to resolve it as one of these two, rather than some other species of whale). (If you are have an opinion about using that as a covariate please feel free to comment but it is not the focus of my main question.)

The Q-Q plot looks good and the statistics in NoBins.txt look fine. The right truncation distance corresponds to detection probability of around 0.15, which I recall as a recent alternative to the “right truncate 5%” rule. Answering my own question #1 above, I believe this detection function is reasonable and that the right tail is not excessively long. How about question #2? Unfortunately the detection function histogram shows the big spikes. When I show this plot to people they often express strong dissatisfaction with the spikes and sometimes question whether the detection function makes any sense at all. Now the alternative:

The attached Bins.pdf and Bins.txt show a detection function for which I have defined explicit breaks defined at angular distances that enclose the heaping angles. These vary a bit because sometimes the bin is 5 degrees, sometimes 1 degree, and so on. I can explain the details fully if desired. Anyway, we can see here that the bin heights conform much better what we expect: decreasing detection probability with distance. This occurs as the spikes of sightings are “spread out” across the bin ranges. This also draws some comments but seems to prompt fewer objections than the big spikes.

This Q-Q plot also looks good and the statistics in Bins.txt are nearly identical to NoBins.txt. So my question to you, the basis for this entire email:

Dear Distance users,

During boat-based line transect surveys, distances were estimated using reticule binoculars counting divisions downwards from the horizon. In some cases when facing shore the nearest land mass was used instead of the horizon. I have attempted to convert these into radial distances using R following Lerczak and Hobbs 1998: Calculating sighting distances from angular readings during shipboard, aerial and shore-based marine mammal surveys. Mar. Mam. Sci. 14(3):590-599 (Appendix 1).

For horizon-based estimations I used the formula in Buckland et al 2001 Introduction to Distance sampling and am quite confident with the results. However I am less confident with my calculations for the shore-based estimates due to my limited maths skills. I think I may be going wrong when calculating some of the angles but also in Lerczack & Hobbs they use include ‘U’ and ‘W’ in D0 equation 4, Appendix 1 but with no mention previously to what these values should be. And so I ignored them!  The distances look larger than I would expect. Does anyone have a formula/R code that they could share to calculate distance from a known distance to shore or could any R users have a look at the following code to see where I’ve gone wrong? Any guidance would be much appreciated, this has taken a ridiculously long time! Code below ad Lerczak and Hobbs paper attached:

  #########################################################

# CALCULATING RADIAL DISTANCE USING RETICLES FROM SHORE #

#########################################################

# formula taken from Lerczak & Hobbs 1998. Should be in radians.

shore.dist<-read.csv("U:/College of Natural Sciences/Research Data/R28W07-201908-DemoZone/Data/Mammals/LT Surveys/Reticule corrections/CorrectedDistancesJW_v2.csv")

library("aspace")

ret.deg<-0.05625 # 5 mil= ret.deg. one reticle= 5 mil. 1 mil=0.05625 degrees

mil.deg2rad<- (0.05625*pi)/180

D <- list()

# shore.dist[i,11]- reticule number, shore.dist[i,9]- distance to land, shore.dist[i,13]- observer height

for(i in 1:nrow(shore.dist)){

   hor.angle2<-(shore.dist[i,11]*5)*mil.deg2rad  # no. reticles*5= no. mils*0.05625 to convert to degrees.

  gamma<-shore.dist[i,9]/6370

  L0<-sqrt((6370^2)+((6370+shore.dist[i,13])^2)-(2*6370)*(6370+shore.dist[i,13])*(cos(gamma)))

  beta<-acos(((2*shore.dist[i,13]*6370)+(shore.dist[i,13]^2)+(L0^2))/(2*(6370+shore.dist[i,13])*L0))-hor.angle2 #change to radians

angle.sight<-sinpi(sin(beta)*(d0/6370))

  D[[i]]=angle.sight*6370}

>
>
>
> All is not perfect however. The aircraft have large bubble windows but on NARWSS surveys there are only two window observers; there is no belly observer, nor a second team, precluding an mrds analysis. That is ok; we can do a single-team analysis. Of greater concern, the protocol asks observers to spend less time guarding the trackline than is proper for distance sampling, and more time looking in the distance for whales. This is intended to maximize the number of right whales they can find and go photograph, Unfortunately histograms of sighting distances suggest this practice causes them to miss some animals along the trackline. We have dealt with this problem with left truncation.
>
>
>
> And there is another caveat, the one I would like your opinion on:
>
>
>
> Because NARWSS has flown so many surveys (roughly 0.5 million linear km on effort) and the protocol allows observers to spend some of their time looking into the distance, they have obtained quite a few sightings at distances that might be farther than is typical for aerial surveys flown at 750 ft. Assuming these sightings can be incorporated into a detection function reasonably well, I would like to retain as many of them as possible, as I am trying to fit seasonal density surface GAMs with multiple covariates. These GAMs work best when many sightings are available.
>
>
>
> The complication is that there is some heaping of vertical angles, which is exacerbated by the relatively large angles obtained for distant sightings. Below 80 degrees, there was a tendency to heap at 5 degree increments. This stopped at 80 degrees but the inclinometer only had a resolution of 1 degree, yielding measurements of 80, 81, 82, and so on. At those extreme angles, a 1 degree angular difference corresponds to a large linear distance range on the ground.
>
>
>
> (Now, some of you are probably already thinking that this is crazy, trying to utilize aerial sightings with vertical angles of 80 degrees and even higher. Feel free to tell me so, but please bear with me and see what results. Then tell me again it is crazy, if desired.)
>
>
>
> The attached heaping.png histogram of sightings of right whales by distance shows what I’m talking about. The x axis is distance in meters; the y axis is count of sightings. The "spikes" in this histogram correspond to vertical angles which I have labelled in red. At 80 degrees and higher, the clustering that occurs around the spike results from variations in aircraft altitude, not in the sighing angle. If the aircraft were flown at precisely the target altitude at all times, the clusters would shrink to perfect spikes at the heaping distances, with nothing at intermediate distances. Below 80 degrees, the clustering around the 5 degree increments results both from variation in altitude and from not all measurements being rounded to 5 degrees.
>
>
>
> From the height of these spikes, you can see why I would want to retain them, if possible: they represent a very large number of sightings that I’d like to make available to the spatial modeling stage, if possible. In the right whale example, there are roughly 700 sightings in the 80-87 degree range, out of 1700 total. I am reluctant to discard many of those, if they can be reasonably retained. This leads to two questions:
>
>
>
> 1. Do these represent a long tail that is hard to model well and should thus be truncated?
>
>
>
> 2. Assuming they can be modeled reasonably, should I fit detection functions with explicit breaks to account for the heaping, or not?
>
>
>
> To address the first question, let’s assume the answer is Yes and examine resulting detection functions to see if they are reasonable. For this example, I’ll use a detection function for fin and sei whales rather than for right whales. The attached LeftTrunc.pdf shows the sightings I used. I left truncated these at 62 m, an angle of 15 degrees at 750 ft, based on examining this plot. This is an area of the trackline that was not sufficiently attended. The red bar represents the truncated sightings.
>
>
>
> I right truncated at 3738 m, an angle of 86.5 degrees, with the intent of enclosing the bin that was centered on 86 degrees. Conceptually, this assumes the error in angular measurement was spread evenly between 85.5 and 86.5 degrees. This discarded 341 sightings, 11% of the total, that were beyond this distance, leaving 2608 left, 87% of the total. This right-truncates considerably more than 5%, which is suggested in various places as a general rule.
>
>
>
> The attached NoBins.pdf and NoBins.txt show the resulting detection function. I used the species identification as an MCDS covariate to deal with the problem that many sightings were reported as “fin or sei whale” because observers are less likely to be able to distinguish between the two as distance increases (but are still able to resolve it as one of these two, rather than some other species of whale). (If you are have an opinion about using that as a covariate please feel free to comment but it is not the focus of my main question.)
>
>
>
> The Q-Q plot looks good and the statistics in NoBins.txt look fine. The right truncation distance corresponds to detection probability of around 0.15, which I recall as a recent alternative to the “right truncate 5%” rule. Answering my own question #1 above, I believe this detection function is reasonable and that the right tail is not excessively long. How about question #2? Unfortunately the detection function histogram shows the big spikes. When I show this plot to people they often express strong dissatisfaction with the spikes and sometimes question whether the detection function makes any sense at all. Now the alternative:
>
>
>
> The attached Bins.pdf and Bins.txt show a detection function for which I have defined explicit breaks defined at angular distances that enclose the heaping angles. These vary a bit because sometimes the bin is 5 degrees, sometimes 1 degree, and so on. I can explain the details fully if desired. Anyway, we can see here that the bin heights conform much better what we expect: decreasing detection probability with distance. This occurs as the spikes of sightings are “spread out” across the bin ranges. This also draws some comments but seems to prompt fewer objections than the big spikes.
>
>
>
> This Q-Q plot also looks good and the statistics in Bins.txt are nearly identical to NoBins.txt. So my question to you, the basis for this entire email:
>
>
>
> Assuming these detection functions are reasonable, which should I use? The bins seem more aesthetically pleasing to some people—I myself have a hard time viewing the histogram spike favorably. But the resulting statistics are essentially the same, with the “NoBins” approach scoring slightly better on the KS and CvM tests and having slightly lower CVs. So what do you think?
>
>
>
> Thanks for reading and any comments you wish to provide,
>
>
>
> Jason
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How to set up multipliers for point transect data?
messages.body_plain:
Nick, that is handled by the ‘effort’ variable.  If a point is surveyed x times, then the survey effort is x.  When some points are surveyed more times than others, it must be assumed that the number of times a point is surveyed is independent of animal density, so normally, it is good practice to keep the number of visits constant, at least within a stratum.

Steve Buckland

The best way to organise your data for import into Distance is described
at this link:

https://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/preparing-your-data-for-use-in-distance-august-2015/

It is easiest if you arrange your data by:

stratum name, stratum area, transect name, transect length,
perpendicular distance

there are other fields you can include, perhaps species name if it is a
multispecies survey.  But the basic information should be ordered in
this manner.  It can then be imported into Distance.
